1                                              INTRODUCTION

2              Now on the fourth complaint in this matter, Plaintiffs Sarah Isgur, Eddie Edwards, and

3    Richard Repp seek yet again to hold Defendant Meta Platforms, Inc. (“Meta”) liable for the

4    takeover of their Facebook accounts by malicious third parties. This Court previously dismissed

5    Plaintiffs’ Second Amended Complaint (“SAC”; Dkt. No. 37) for failure to state claims, and

6    Plaintiffs’ attempt to replead their claims in their Third Amended Complaint (the “TAC”; Dkt.

7    No. 48) fares no better. The TAC repeats many of the allegations that this Court found deficient

8    when dismissing the SAC. The Plaintiffs also pivot to a “license revocation” theory, which this

9    Court dismissed as insufficiently pled in the SAC. Isgur, et al. v. Meta Platforms, Inc., 2026 WL

10   194640, at *4-5 (N.D. Cal. Jan. 26, 2026). Despite getting another bite at the apple, Plaintiffs’

11   license revocation theory still fails. Accordingly, the Court should dismiss Plaintiffs’ claims with

12   prejudice.

13             Just like the SAC, the heart of Plaintiffs’ TAC is the notion that, after third-party bad

14   actors took over Plaintiffs’ accounts, Meta did not promptly restore Plaintiffs’ access to their

15   accounts. See, e.g., TAC ¶¶ 2-3, 13-14, 40-41. And, just as in the SAC, Plaintiffs attempt to hold

16   Meta liable for the misconduct of these third-party bad actors. But this Court already ruled that

17   “[i]nsofar as the SAC and any TAC attempts to allege that Meta is liable under its TOS for (1)

18   any third-party hacker behavior or (2) responsible for immediately remedying third party

19   behavior, such claims are not actionable.” Isgur, 2026 WL 194640, at *6.

20             Plaintiffs endeavor to circumvent this admonition by focusing on their previously (and

21   still) inadequately pled “license revocation” theory. The TOS state that when users share, post, or

22   upload content they grant Meta a “non-exclusive, transferable, sub-licensable, royalty-free, and

23   worldwide license” and that the “license will end when your content is deleted from our

24   systems.” Ex. A at 8 §3.3.1; Ex. B at 9 §3.3.2.1 Plaintiffs argue that this language means users

25   can revoke—at any time—Meta’s license to their content by deleting the content. TAC ¶¶ 7, 12,

26   35-37, 146-48. They further contend that because locked-out users cannot revoke Meta’s license,

1    Meta has violated the TOS and is liable for breach of contract (Count I). TAC ¶¶ 146-53. But,

2    contrary to what Plaintiffs claim, the TOS do not promise that locked-out users can delete their

3    content. Nor do the TOS establish that user-deletion of content, on its own, terminates Meta’s

4    license. Such a reading contradicts the plain language of the TOS, which (1) do not impose any

5    obligation on Meta to facilitate deletion of content by locked-out users, and (2) provide that Meta

6    retains a license to content for as long as it resides on Meta’s systems, and that there are

7    circumstances in which Meta may continue to store content after it has been deleted by users.

8            Plaintiffs attempt to evade the plain language of the TOS by claiming that Plaintiffs’

9    inability to terminate Meta’s license is a breach of the implied covenant of good faith and fair

10   dealing (Count II). This claim fails for three independent reasons. First, an implied covenant

11   claim cannot be used to impose obligations not contained in the contractual language, and

12   because the TOS contain no promise of license revocation, the implied covenant claim cannot

13   manufacture one. Second, Plaintiffs cannot plausibly allege the bad faith required to maintain an

14   implied covenant claim—none of their bad faith allegations reflect the required conscious and

15   deliberate intent to frustrate the contract. Third, Plaintiffs’ assertion that Meta violated their

16   contractual expectations by retaining the license while Plaintiffs lacked account access, TAC

17   ¶ 155, cannot be squared with the TOS, which make clear that Meta’s license exists for the broad

18   purpose of “providing and improving [its] Products and services,” Ex. A at 7 §3.3.1, Ex. B at 8

19   §3.3.1, not solely to facilitate Plaintiffs’ own use of the platform.

20           Finally, Plaintiffs’ claim for violation of California’s Unfair Competition Law, Cal. Bus.

21   & Prof. § 17200 et seq. (“UCL”) (Count III) fails as well. Plaintiffs have not adequately alleged

22   any economic injury sufficient to grant them standing to bring any of their UCL claims.

23   Moreover, Plaintiffs’ attempt to argue a breach of the “unlawful” prong of the UCL fails because

24   Plaintiffs base this claim on Meta’s alleged breach of contract. It is well-established that

25   Plaintiffs cannot base a claim under the unlawful prong of the UCL on an alleged breach of

26   contract. Nor can Plaintiffs’ claim under the “unfairness” prong of the UCL survive—among

27   other reasons, the unfair business practices alleged overlap entirely with the business practices

28   alleged under the unlawful prong of the UCL, and in such a situation, a claim under the unfair

4                                       PROCEDURAL HISTORY

5            Plaintiff Isgur filed her original Complaint on September 18, 2024. Dkt. No. 1. Meta

6     timely filed a motion to dismiss on November 19, 2024. Dkt. No. 22. In lieu of opposing the

7     motion, Plaintiff Isgur filed an Amended Complaint on January 21, 2025. Dkt. No. 27. Just four

8     days before Meta’s March 24, 2025 deadline to respond, Plaintiff Isgur notified Meta that she

9     may seek to amend her Complaint a second time to bring in additional clients she had recruited.

10    Dkt. No. 31. Plaintiff Isgur then sought leave to file Plaintiffs’ SAC, Dkt. No. 35, which was

11    granted on June 2, 2025, Dkt. No. 36. Plaintiffs filed the SAC on June 4, 2025. Dkt. 37. Meta

12    filed its motion to dismiss the SAC on July 17, 2025, Dkt. 40. On January 26, 2026, the Court

13    granted Meta’s motion to dismiss in part, dismissing each of Plaintiffs’ causes of action with

14    leave to amend. Isgur, 2026 WL 194640, at *11. On February 25, 2026, a subset of Plaintiffs

15    identified in the SAC filed their TAC. Dkt. No. 48.

16                                            BACKGROUND

17           A.      Meta Promotes The Security Of Its Services.
18           Meta operates Facebook, an online service that helps users build community, discover,

19    connect, and share messages, photos, videos, and links to other content. Ex. A at 2; Ex. B at 2,

20    Overview. As stated in the TOS, “[p]eople will only build community on Meta Products if they

21    feel safe and secure,” and Meta “work[s] hard to maintain the security. . . of [its] Products and

22    services.” Ex. A at 3 § 1; Ex. B at 4 § 1.5. When users lose control over their accounts, the

23    locked-out users may miss out on Facebook’s content, and other users who interact with the

24    accounts that have been taken over may have bad experiences. See e.g., TAC ¶¶ 16, 56-58, 99-

25    100.

26           Meta “[p]romote[s] the safety, security, and integrity of [its] services.” For instance,

27    Meta’s TOS describe that Meta:

11    them. Id. ¶¶ 38 n.6, 54, 70, 72, 78, 87. For example, Meta alerts users of unusual account

12    activities, and Facebook’s log-in page provides information on “account recovery options” for

16           Plaintiffs allege they lost access to their Facebook accounts due to the conduct of third-

17    party bad actors, not Meta. Plaintiff Isgur alleges that her Facebook account was “hacked by an

18    unknown user” on June 21, 2023. TAC ¶ 52. This unknown user “immediately changed the

19    password, mobile phone number, and email address associated with her accounts.” Id. Likewise,

20    Plaintiff Repp alleges that between September 19-22, 2024, an “unknown user” took over his

21    account. TAC ¶¶ 83-86. Similarly, Plaintiff Edwards alleges that his “account was hacked by an

22    unknown user” on March 5, 2025. TAC ¶ 64. Plaintiff Edwards has since regained access to his

23    account. TAC ¶¶ 78-79.

25    Facebook. Plaintiffs allege they contacted Meta through various channels seeking to recover

27    at restoring account access. Id. Nevertheless, Plaintiffs now assert that, if they could not regain

28    account access, they would “prefer[] for Meta to return [their] personal content and provide

3            B.      Meta Has A License To User Content That Ends When It Is Deleted From
                     Meta’s Systems.
4

5            Plaintiffs seek to hold Meta liable for their lockouts under a “license revocation” theory

6     of liability, which focuses on the license that Facebook users, such as Plaintiffs, grant Meta. As

7     stated in the TOS, when users “share, post, or upload” content to their accounts, they grant Meta

8     a “non-exclusive, transferable, sub-licensable, royalty-free, and worldwide license.” Ex. A at 8 §

9     3.3.1; Ex. B at 9 § 3.3.2; TAC ¶¶ 6-7, 35-36, 146-47. The license gives Meta authority to “host,

10    use, distribute, modify, run, copy, publicly perform or display, translate, and create derivative

11    works of [the] content.” Ex. A at 8 § 3.3.1; Ex. B at 9 § 3.3.2. Meta’s license exists “for the

12    purposes of providing and improving [Meta’s] Products and services,” including Facebook. Ex.

13    A at 7 § 3.3.1; Ex. B at 8 § 3.3.1. The TOS state that Meta’s license ends when the “content is

14    deleted from [Meta’s] systems.” Ex. A at 8 § 3.3.1; Ex. B at 9 § 3.3.2.

15           The TOS distinguish between user deletion of content and the deletion of content from

16    Meta’s systems. The latter–Meta’s deletion of content from Meta’s systems–is what ends Meta’s

3             B.     Plaintiffs Cannot Base An Unlawful Claim On A Breach Of Contract.
4             Even if Plaintiffs were able to allege an economic injury sufficient to bring a UCL claim,

5     they have not sufficiently alleged that Meta’s conduct is unlawful. The unlawful prong “borrows

6     violations of other laws and treats them as unlawful practices that the unfair competition law

7     makes independently actionable.” Hadley v. Kellogg Sales Co., 243 F. Supp. 3d 1074, 1094

8     (N.D. Cal. 2017). Plaintiffs assert that Meta violated the unlawful prong of the UCL “by

9     violating California contract law.” TAC ¶ 178. But it is well established that a plaintiff cannot

10    base a claim under the unlawful prong of the UCL on an alleged breach of contract. Ndulue v.

11    Fremont-Rideout Health Grp., 770 F. App’x 335, 338 (9th Cir. 2019) (“Because a breach of

12    contract cannot satisfy the ‘unlawful’ prong of California’s UCL, [defendant] is entitled to

14    (E.D. Cal. Oct. 25, 2024) (dismissing UCL unlawful claim where plaintiff “does not go beyond

15    alleging common law contract violations”); Wright v. Charles Schwab & Co., Inc., 2021 WL

16    1056838, at *8 (N.D. Cal. Mar. 18, 2021) (dismissing UCL claim because “[t]he breach-of-

18    more”); Shroyer v. New Cingular Wireless Servs., 622 F.3d 1035, 1044 (9th Cir. 2010) (“a

21    4th 638, 645 (2008) (finding a breach of contract is not itself an unlawful act for purposes of the

22    UCL).

23            Because Plaintiffs do not allege any violation of any other law in connection with their

Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13
                                               California’s UCL prohibits “any unlawful, unfair, or fraudulent business act or practice.”
                                  14
                                       Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 17200. A UCL claim may only be brought by “a person who has
                                  15
                                       suffered injury in fact and has lost money or property as a result of the unfair competition.” Id. at
                                  16

                                  17   § 17204. Plaintiffs must therefore “demonstrate some form of economic injury.” Kwikset Corp. v.

                                  18   Superior Court, 51 Cal. 4th 310, 323 (2011). For example, a “plaintiff may (1) surrender in a

                                  19   transaction more, or acquire in a transaction less, than he or she otherwise would have; (2) have a
                                  20   present or future property interest diminished; (3) be deprived of money or property to which he or
                                  21
                                       she has a cognizable claim; or (4) be required to enter into a transaction, costing money or
                                  22
                                       property, that would otherwise have been unnecessary.” Id. This list is non-exhaustive. Id.

                                  16

                                  17   theories: (1) unfair benefit-of-the-bargain; (2) diminished value of personal information; and (3)

                                  26   the Hon. William Alsup held in Bass v. Facebook, “[t]hat the information has external value, but

                                  27   no economic value to plaintiff, cannot serve to establish that plaintiff has personally” suffered an
                                  28
                                       economic injury. 394 F. Supp. 3d 1024, 1040 (N.D. Cal. 2019). And, as explained by Judge Pitts

                                   1

                                       (2022)). Plaintiffs have not alleged any attempt or intention to participate in the market in the

                                                                                         17

                                   1

                                   3   CV-03455-WHO, 2014 WL 1411249, at *2 (N.D. Cal. Apr. 11, 2014) (Orrick, J.). In cases where

                                       without regard to the parties’ intent, in order to avoid unjust enrichment.” Id. (citation omitted).

                                   9

                                  10   cannot assert any substantive claims against a defendant.” In re Actimmune Marketing Litig., No.

                                  11   C-08-02376-MHP, 2009 WL 3740648, at *16 (N.D. Cal. Nov. 6, 2009) (Patel, J.). Since I have
                                  12   already dismissed each of plaintiffs’ previous causes of action in this case, it follows that this

 United States District Court




                                  13
                                       cause of action must be dismissed too. But, more important to the claims as currently pleaded,

                                       enforceable express contract.” Durrell v. Sharp Healthcare, 183 Cal. App. 4th 1350, 1370 (2010).

                                  18   recovery at the pleading stage . . . and even inconsistent claims alleging both the existence and the

                                  23

                                  24

                                  25   18, 2020) (Hamilton, J.) (citation omitted). Plaintiffs allege the existence of a contract throughout

24   “content has been used by others . . . and they have not deleted it,” the content will not be deleted

25   from Meta’s systems, and Meta’s license continues. MTD Ex. 1 at 10–11; MTD Ex. 5 at 8–9.

27   restrict Meta’s ability to “investigate . . . violations of [Meta’s] terms and policies.” MTD Ex. 1 at
